notes.1a: Candidates struggled on this first part question. There were a wide range of incorrect answers here. Many candidates chose metals as their answer with the most common incorrect answer being ‘calcium’. Some candidates incorrectly thought the answer was ‘oxygen’.
notes.1b: Candidates did slightly better on this question and could identify a transition element.
notes.1c: This chemical test recall question was well answered.
notes.1e: Candidates found this question very straight forward and knew that copper is used in electrical wiring.
notes.1f: Many candidates did not know the reactivity series of metals and thought the answer was copper.
notes.1g: Candidates struggled with this question and did not know that a diatomic molecule which is a solid at room temperature and pressure is iodine.
notes.1h: Candidates again struggled with this question. They did not have much knowledge of the blast furnace.
notes.1hi: Most candidates could answer this question correctly.
notes.2ai: Most candidates could state the correct chemical name from the formula given. However, there were a few candidates that incorrectly thought that the chemical name was ‘magnesium sulfite’ or ‘magnesium sulfur oxide’.
notes.2aii: Most candidates could work out the correct answer for this calculation using the data given. Some candidates got the data mixed up and so did not gain credit . Some candidates were a factor of 10 or 100 out.
notes.2aiii: Candidates struggled with this solubility rules question. More work needs to be done on learning the solubility rules. Candidates struggled to work out that the correct answer was ‘sodium hydroxide’.
notes.2b: Candidates found this question very challenging and could not recall the chemical test for iodide ions. Some candidates got confused with other chemical tests. A few candidates put the correct reagent but then the wrong colour of precipitate.
notes.2c: Many candidates could show the correct electronic configuration of a potassium ion ; fewer knew the correct charge on this ion.
notes.2d: Candidates found this ‘kinetic particle model’ question much harder. In quite a few cases they misinterpreted the rubric. Some candidates got the terms ‘separation’ and ‘arrangement’ mixed up and wrote down a correct answer for arrangement and not separation. Candidates also wrongly compared states. They talked about ways of changing the state of the solid and so did not achieve any credit . In many cases candidates confused bulk properties with particle movement. Lots of candidates described incorrectly the speed or distance between the particles.
notes.2e: Candidates struggled with this question and found it very challenging. Many candidates did not know ‘one source of phosphate ions’.
notes.2f: Candidates did reasonably well on this question. Most could draw the bonding pairs of electrons between the oxygen and hydrogen atoms. Putting extra electrons on the hydrogen atoms was the most common mistake.
notes.3ai: This question was not very well answered. A few candidates knew that the correct answer was ‘different boiling points’.
notes.3aii: Candidates struggled with this question on the separation of petroleum. Few candidates gained full credit marks here. Candidates struggled with this separation process and many incorrectly answered using the process of cracking.
notes.3aiii: Candidates struggled to correctly name the process.
notes.3aiv: Most candidates answered this uses question correctly. This was an improvement on previous years where candidates had struggled with the uses of substances in the fractional distillation of petroleum.
notes.3bi: This was found to be the hardest question on this paper and l ots of incorrect answers were seen . Candidates struggled to ‘draw the displayed formula of a molecule of ethanoic acid’. Many formula s had the incorrect number of carbon atoms. Some candidates omitted to put the covalent bond between the oxygen and hydrogen of the carboxylic acid functional group.
notes.3bii: Candidates also found this question very challenging and many could not name the salt correctly. Most struggled with the ‘ethanoate’ part of the name of the salt.
notes.3c: This question was very well answered.
notes.3d: Many candidates struggled to state the two ways of manufacturing ethanol. A significant number of candidates did not answer this question.
notes.3ei: Most candidates were able to deduce the molecular formula of the given compound correctly.
notes.3eii: Candidates needed to be more specific in answering this question. Many candidates gave ‘ double bond ’ in their answer but then omitted to mention that it was a carbon carbon double bond . Some candidates misinterpreted this question and thought that the question was asking about the meaning of the term ‘unsaturated solution’.
notes.4aii: Candidates did much better on this question. Most knew how to work out the number of protons present in each isotope and could give the correct answers. Some struggled with the number of neutrons and electrons and some got these mixed up.
notes.4ai: This question was not well answered by many candidates. Many candidates did not know why nitrogen is in Group V of the Periodic Table.
notes.4bi: Candidates found this part question very challenging and there were few correct answers seen. Common incorrect answers were ‘factories’ and ‘combustion of fossil fuels’.
notes.4bii: This was a very well answered question. Most candidates could correctly balance the given equation.
notes.4biii: ‘Ionic bonding’, ‘single bonds’ or ‘double bonds’ were all seen as incorrect answers to this question.
notes.4biv: Candidates found this question very challenging. Many incorrectly thought that nitrogen dioxide was a basic oxide.
notes.4c: Candidates struggled to calculate the relative formula mass of the given compound and there were many incorrect answers seen. Instead of using the number of atoms in the given formula a lot of candidates used the atomic number of the element which gave, incorrectly, very big numbers for the answer.
notes.5a: Most candidates answered this question correctly. However, some candidates thought that ‘hydrogen’ was given off instead of ‘carbon dioxide’ or ‘water’.
notes.5b: Many candidates struggled with this question. They struggled to describe how to make pure, dry crystals of the pure salt from an aqueous solution of the salt. Many candidates just used ‘heat’ but did not state correctly that heat needed to be applied until the ‘point of crystallisation’ or ‘until crystals were seen’. Most candidates forgot to ‘filter’ off the excess magnesium oxide at the start or ‘dry with filter paper’ at the end of the process.
notes.5ci: Candidates performed well on this question . Many could label correctly the ‘electrolyte’ and the ‘anode’. However, some incorrectly label led the wires. ( ii) Many candidates found this a very challenging question. Few could name the product formed at each electrode. Some go t ‘bromide’ confused with the correct ‘bromine’. A few candidates misread the question and thought that the electrolysis was in aqueous solution and so used hydrogen as one of their answers.
notes.5d: Candidates found this question challenging. They struggled to use the given data to identify the two compounds that were simple molecules and were enable to give reasons why they were simple molecules .
notes.6bi: The majority of candidates were able to answer this question correctly. This question had the highest number of correct answers .
notes.6a: Most candidates could select the correct chemical change in this question.
notes.6bii: Candidates found this question slightly more challenging. The most common incorrect answer was experiment 2 where candidates got mixed up with the temperature changes for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction.
notes.6biii: Candidates found this question more challenging. M ost candidates could label the ‘reactants’ and ‘products’ the correct way around ; far fewer could label the ‘vertical axis’ .
notes.7a: Most candidates struggled with this question on the treatment of domestic water. Hardly any candidates knew the stages. Most candidates did not gain any credit .
notes.7b: Candidates also struggled on this question. There were very few correct answers seen. Candidates did not know a chemical test for the presence of water.
notes.7c: Candidates struggled with this question and many did not know one harmful effect of the given air pollutants. Some candidates put down ‘harmful’ which was in the stem of the question.
notes.8ai: The majority of candidates were able to answer this question correctly.
notes.8aii: Candidates found this question more challenging. Many candidates just talked about decreasing the amount of metal or volume of sulfuric acid used which was incorrect.
notes.8bi: Many candidates did not know the correct flame colour for lithium ions.
notes.8bii: Most candidates did not know the ion that all aqueous alkalis contain.
notes.8biii: Many candidates did not know the colour of thymolphthalein in an aqueous alkali. Many candidates thought that it was ‘red’ or ‘yellow’.
notes.8ci: Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.8cii: Candidates struggled on this question. There were very few correct answers seen. ‘High melting point’ or ‘conducts electricity’ were the most common incorrect answers.
notes.8d: Most candidates answered this question correctly. They knew at least one property that was typical of metals.
